query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small, trace amount of boron (around 0.5 at%) during synthesis of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo will modify the local bonding environment—especially at grain boundaries—to ease dislocation nucleation and movement, thereby enhancing room‐temperature compressive plasticity while largely preserving high yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, a disordered BCC solid solution with high Mo content, which exhibits very high yield strength (~1719 MPa) but limited plasticity due to the large electronegativity difference induced by Mo.
generation.intervention: Add approximately 0.5 at% boron uniformly into the NbZrTiHfMo alloy during melting/synthesis.
generation.conditions: Samples are to be produced under identical processing and homogenization heat‐treatment conditions and then tested in room‐temperature compression.
generation.structural_mediator: Local grain boundary chemistry and short‐range atomic order; boron segregation at grain boundaries and near dislocation cores is expected to reduce local bond stiffness associated with high Mo content.
generation.mechanism: Boron, as a trace interstitial, is predicted to preferentially segregate to grain boundaries and certain dislocation sites. This segregation reduces local electronegativity differences arising from Mo, decreases the barriers for dislocation motion, and improves grain boundary cohesion. The net effect is an increase in plasticity without a dramatic loss in yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The boron-modified alloy is expected to show a modest yield strength reduction (around 5–10% lower than 1719 MPa) but a significant increase in ductility (an increase in compressive strain before fracture to above 15% compared to the current brittle behavior).
generation.baseline: Standard equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo showing high compressive yield strength (~1719 MPa) and low room-temperature plasticity.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected for boron additions up to approximately 1 at%; higher concentrations may lead to formation of brittle boride phases that would be deleterious to both strength and ductility.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extrapolates beneficial interstitial effects observed in other refractory HEA systems (e.g., trace carbon or boron effects in MoNbTaW alloys as discussed in PMC9586648::web::003) to NbZrTiHfMo. The optimal boron content and its segregation behavior in NbZrTiHfMo remain to be quantified; therefore, the exact balance between preserved yield strength and improved plasticity is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of NbZrTiHfMo alloy samples under controlled identical melting and homogenization conditions – one set as the baseline and another with 0.5 at% boron addition. Prepare specimens for room-temperature compression testing. Use microscopy techniques (TEM/SEM with chemical analysis) to verify uniform boron distribution and absence of brittle boride precipitates.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (grain boundary segregation, phase identification)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in compressive plasticity (i.e., less than a 5% improvement in fracture strain) or if the yield strength falls by more than 15% compared to the baseline, the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, careful microstructural examination of Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr was carried out in the present study using advanced TEM and APT techniques. The results reveal that the homogenized and slow cooled (~10 °C/min) microstructure (Condition (1)) has an ordered B2 phase as the continuous matrix, interspersed with discrete cuboidal-like pockets of a disordered BCC phase. While this microstructure morphologically resembles the γ (fcc) + γ’ (ordered L12) type microstructure observed in many Ni-base superalloys, it is “inverted” in the sense that the continuous matrix phase is the ordered B2 phase, resulting in limited compressive ductility. The ductility of this alloy was substantially increased via microstructural engineering involving controlled annealing treatments, resulting in a phase inversion. Consequently, the hard, ordered B2 compound that forms the continuous phase in Condition (1) is replaced by the more ductile, disordered, BCC phase in Condition (3). The resultant microstructurally-engineered RHEA not only exhibits high yield strength at room temperature (~1345 MPa) and 600 °C (~1423 MPa), but also substantial compressive ductility at room temperature (>20%). Figure 2 shows the X-Ray diffraction patterns. The main phase of the Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy series is a BCC disordered solid solution. The asymmetry of (200) and (211) peaks are shown in the diffraction pattern results from the cored dendritic structure. The composition variation of dendritic and interdendritic areas causes a little difference in the lattice constant. The lattice constants of the Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy series listed in Table 2 are in the range of 3.305 to 3.400 Å calculated by the Nelson–Riley extrapolation function. Referring to the phase diagrams of each binary alloy between Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr, Hf-Mo, and Mo-Zr binary alloys form Mo2Hf and Mo2Zr, respectively, in a certain range of composition even at high temperature. However, these two intermetallic compounds or others do not show up in Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys, which means the high entropy effect has a significant benefit in forming simple BCC solid solution in this alloy system especially at high temperature.

Several theoretical models of solid-solution strengthening have been proposed to explain how different constituent elements affect room-temperature or elevated-temperature strength [,]. We previously designed a RHEA that exhibited higher elevated-temperature strength and discussed the effect of the constituent elements on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys by using the subtraction method []. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add elements such as Mo, which significantly interact with the other elements. For higher elevated-temperature strength, one should add the elements that possess a high melting point such as Mo, Nb, or Ta. For higher ductility, one should add more Nb. With Ti or Zr addition, both the elevated-temperature strength and the density decrease.
